metadata.name: NCERT Class 11 Physics RAG Evaluation Dataset — v2.0 (Fixed Dataset)
metadata.description: Evaluation dataset for the FIXED NCERT Class 11 Physics RAG dataset. Each question includes reference_chunk_id pointing to the specific chunk that should be retrieved. All reference answers are grounded strictly in NCERT textbook content.

how_to_use.retrieval_eval: Query RAG with `question`. Check if `reference_chunk_id` is in top-k retrieved chunks → Recall@k.
how_to_use.answer_eval: Compare system answer to `reference_answer` using ROUGE-L, BERTScore, or LLM judge.
how_to_use.key_concept_eval: Check if all `key_concepts` appear in the system answer.
how_to_use.grading: Use `grading_criteria` for human or LLM-based pass/fail grading.

questions.question: Define 'unit' in the context of measurement. What is the difference between fundamental units and derived units?
questions.reference_answer: A unit is a certain basic, arbitrarily chosen, internationally accepted reference standard used to measure a physical quantity. The result of measurement is expressed as a number accompanied by a unit. Fundamental (or base) units are units defined for the fundamental base quantities (e.g., metre for length, kilogram for mass). Derived units are combinations of base units used to express all other physical quantities. A complete set of base and derived units forms a system of units.
questions.grading_criteria: Must define 'unit' as a reference standard; distinguish fundamental from derived; mention the SI system.

questions.question: Name the seven base quantities in the SI system and their corresponding SI units.
questions.reference_answer: The seven SI base quantities and their units are: (1) Length — metre (m), (2) Mass — kilogram (kg), (3) Time — second (s), (4) Electric current — ampere (A), (5) Thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K), (6) Amount of substance — mole (mol), (7) Luminous intensity — candela (cd).
questions.grading_criteria: All 7 quantities named with correct units.

questions.question: What are significant figures? State the rules for counting significant figures in a measured quantity.
questions.reference_answer: Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that are known reliably, plus the first uncertain digit. Rules: (1) All non-zero digits are significant. (2) Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. (3) Leading zeros are not significant. (4) Trailing zeros in a decimal number are significant. (5) Trailing zeros without a decimal point are ambiguous.
questions.grading_criteria: Must define significant figures and give at least 3 correct rules.

questions.question: Each side of a cube is measured to be 7.203 m. Calculate the volume of the cube to appropriate significant figures.
questions.reference_answer: Volume = (7.203)³ = 373.714... m³. The measured length has 4 significant figures, so volume = 373.7 m³.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct calculation; answer rounded to 4 sig figs: 373.7 m³.

questions.question: What is dimensional analysis? Describe two of its main applications.
questions.reference_answer: Dimensional analysis uses the principle of homogeneity — all terms in a valid physical equation must have the same dimensions. Applications: (1) Checking correctness of equations. (2) Deriving relationships between physical quantities. (3) Converting units from one system to another.
questions.grading_criteria: Must explain homogeneity and give at least 2 valid applications.

questions.question: Distinguish between distance and displacement. Can displacement be zero when distance is non-zero?
questions.reference_answer: Distance is the total path length traversed, always positive and scalar. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from initial to final position with direction; it is a vector. Displacement can be zero when distance is non-zero — e.g., completing a round trip returns to the start point, so displacement = 0 but distance > 0.
questions.grading_criteria: Clearly distinguish scalar vs vector nature; correct example of zero displacement with non-zero distance.

questions.question: What does the slope and the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.reference_answer: Slope of a v-t graph = Δv/Δt = instantaneous acceleration. Positive slope = positive acceleration; negative slope = deceleration. Area under the v-t curve between two instants = displacement during that interval. Area above time axis = positive displacement; below = negative displacement.
questions.grading_criteria: Slope = acceleration AND area = displacement both correctly stated.

questions.question: Write the three equations of motion for uniformly accelerated motion and define all terms.
questions.reference_answer: (1) v = v₀ + at; (2) x = v₀t + ½at²; (3) v² = v₀² + 2ax. Here v₀ = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = uniform acceleration, t = elapsed time, x = displacement.
questions.grading_criteria: All three equations correctly stated with all variables defined.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity 20 m/s. Find (a) the maximum height reached and (b) the time to reach maximum height. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.reference_answer: (a) At max height v=0. v² = v₀² - 2gh → 0 = 400 - 20h → h = 20 m. (b) v = v₀ - gt → 0 = 20 - 10t → t = 2 s.
questions.grading_criteria: h = 20 m and t = 2 s with correct working.

questions.question: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity? Give two examples of each.
questions.reference_answer: Scalar: only magnitude (e.g., mass, temperature). Vector: magnitude + direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, force). Scalars obey ordinary algebra; vectors obey vector addition laws.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct distinction with valid examples.

questions.question: State the triangle law and parallelogram law of vector addition.
questions.reference_answer: Triangle law: Two vectors placed head-to-tail; the vector from the tail of the first to the head of the second is the resultant. Parallelogram law: Two vectors placed as adjacent sides of a parallelogram; the diagonal from the common point is the resultant.
questions.grading_criteria: Both laws correctly stated; resultant correctly identified.

questions.question: Show that the trajectory of a projectile is parabolic.
questions.reference_answer: x = v₀cosθ · t, so t = x/(v₀cosθ). y = v₀sinθ · t - ½gt². Substituting: y = (tanθ)x - g/(2v₀²cos²θ)·x², which is y = ax - bx² — a parabola.
questions.grading_criteria: Must derive y = ax - bx² by eliminating t.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at 30° with initial speed 40 m/s. Find range, maximum height, and time of flight. (g = 10 m/s²)
State Newton's three laws of motion.
questions.reference_answer: First Law: A body remains at rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force (law of inertia). Second Law: F = dp/dt = ma (net force = rate of change of momentum). Third Law: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction; forces always occur in pairs on different bodies.
questions.grading_criteria: All three laws correctly stated.

questions.question: Why does a cricket player lower their hands while catching a ball? Explain using Newton's second law.
questions.reference_answer: By extending the catching motion, the player increases the time Δt over which the ball decelerates to zero. From F = Δp/Δt, since momentum change is fixed, a larger Δt means smaller force F — reducing injury risk. This applies the impulse-momentum theorem.
questions.grading_criteria: Must use F = Δp/Δt and explain that increasing time reduces force.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of linear momentum and the condition for it to hold.
questions.reference_answer: If net external force on a system is zero, total linear momentum is conserved: p_total = constant. Follows from F = dp/dt; if F = 0, p is constant. Holds for isolated systems; internal Newton's third law force pairs cancel.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct condition (zero net external force); explanation via Newton's laws.

questions.question: A 5 kg block on a rough horizontal surface has μₖ = 0.3 and has a 25 N horizontal force applied. Find acceleration. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.reference_answer: N = mg = 50 N. Friction f = μₖN = 15 N. Net force = 25 - 15 = 10 N. a = F_net/m = 10/5 = 2 m/s².
questions.grading_criteria: N=50N, f=15N, a=2 m/s².

questions.question: Define work done by a force. When is work done zero even if force and displacement are both non-zero?
questions.reference_answer: Work W = F·d = Fd cosθ. Work is zero when θ = 90° — force perpendicular to displacement. Examples: centripetal force, normal force on horizontal motion.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct formula W = Fd cosθ; θ = 90° gives zero work.

questions.question: State the work-energy theorem. Is it valid only for constant forces?
questions.reference_answer: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² - ½mv₀². Valid for both constant and variable forces — the calculus proof W = ∫F dx = Δ(½mv²) holds for any force.
questions.grading_criteria: Must state W_net = ΔKE and confirm it holds for variable forces.

questions.question: What is the difference between conservative and non-conservative forces? Why can we define potential energy only for conservative forces?
questions.reference_answer: Conservative force: work is path-independent, closed-loop work = 0 (e.g., gravity). Non-conservative: work depends on path, energy dissipated (e.g., friction). Potential energy requires conservative forces because PE is stored energy that can be fully recovered — non-conservative forces dissipate energy irreversibly as heat.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct distinction; correct explanation that PE requires reversibility/path independence.

questions.question: A 2 kg ball is dropped from rest from height 5 m. Find its kinetic energy and speed just before impact. (g = 10 m/s²)

questions.chapter_title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: What is the centre of mass? Write its mathematical expression for a system of n particles.
questions.reference_answer: Centre of mass is the point where the entire mass of a system can be assumed concentrated for translational motion. R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ / M, where M = total mass.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct definition and formula R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/M.

questions.chapter_title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: Define torque and angular momentum. Write the rotational analogue of Newton's second law.
questions.reference_answer: Torque τ = r × F; magnitude = rF sinθ; unit N·m. Angular momentum L = r × p = Iω; unit kg·m²/s. Rotational Newton's second law: τ_net = dL/dt = Iα.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct definitions of both; τ = Iα stated.

questions.chapter_title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: State the law of conservation of angular momentum and give a real-world example.
questions.reference_answer: If net external torque is zero, L = Iω is conserved. Example: A figure skater pulling arms inward reduces I, so ω increases (spins faster). Also, Kepler's second law (planets sweep equal areas) follows from this conservation.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct statement; valid real-world example.

questions.chapter_title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: A solid cylinder of mass 4 kg and radius 0.3 m has a torque of 3.6 N·m applied about its central axis. Find moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
questions.grading_criteria: I = 0.18 kg·m², α = 20 rad/s².

questions.question: State Newton's universal law of gravitation and define G.
questions.reference_answer: F = Gm₁m₂/r². G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻² (universal gravitational constant, measured by Cavendish).
questions.grading_criteria: Correct formula; value of G; Cavendish mentioned.

questions.question: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion.
questions.reference_answer: (1) Law of Ellipses: planets orbit Sun in ellipses with Sun at one focus. (2) Law of Areas: the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times. (3) Law of Periods: T² ∝ a³ (period squared proportional to semi-major axis cubed).
questions.grading_criteria: All three laws correctly stated.

questions.question: Calculate the escape speed from Earth's surface. (R_E = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.grading_criteria: Formula v_e = √(2gR); answer ≈ 11.2 km/s.

questions.question: How does g vary with (a) altitude above Earth and (b) depth below Earth's surface?
questions.reference_answer: (a) Above: g' ≈ g(1 - 2h/R) for h << R; decreases with altitude (inverse square law). (b) Below: g' = g(1 - d/R); decreases linearly with depth; g = 0 at Earth's centre.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct formula for altitude AND depth; g=0 at centre.

questions.question: Define stress and strain. State Hooke's law.
questions.reference_answer: Stress = F/A (restoring force per unit area); unit: Pa. Strain = ΔL/L (dimensionless ratio of change to original dimension). Hooke's law: within elastic limit, Stress ∝ Strain (Stress = E × Strain).
questions.grading_criteria: Correct definitions (F/A and ΔL/L); Hooke's law with elastic limit.

questions.question: Define Young's modulus, shear modulus, and bulk modulus.
questions.reference_answer: Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/AΔL. Shear modulus G = (F/A)/(Δx/L). Bulk modulus B = -p/(ΔV/V). All have unit N/m² (Pa).
questions.grading_criteria: All three moduli defined with formulas.

questions.question: A wire of length 3 m and area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² is stretched 1 mm by a force of 100 N. Calculate Young's modulus.
questions.grading_criteria: Y = 3 × 10¹¹ Pa with correct formula.

questions.question: Define pressure. State Pascal's law and give one application.
questions.reference_answer: Pressure P = F/A; unit Pa. Pascal's law: pressure applied to enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions. Application: hydraulic press / hydraulic brakes.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct definition; Pascal's law; hydraulic application.

questions.question: State Bernoulli's principle and explain how it accounts for lift on an aircraft wing.
questions.reference_answer: Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = const along a streamline. For an aircraft wing, air moves faster over the curved upper surface → lower pressure above, higher pressure below → net upward lift force.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct equation; faster flow → lower pressure → upward lift.

questions.question: State Archimedes' principle. What is the condition for a body to float?
questions.reference_answer: Archimedes' principle: a submerged body experiences upward buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced (F_b = ρ_fluid × V_sub × g). Body floats when F_b = weight, i.e., average density of body ≤ density of fluid.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct principle; correct floating condition.

questions.question: Distinguish between specific heat capacity and latent heat.
questions.reference_answer: Specific heat capacity c: Q = mcΔT — heat to raise temperature of 1 kg by 1 K. Latent heat L: Q = mL — heat to change phase of 1 kg at constant temperature (no temperature change).
questions.grading_criteria: Specific heat → temperature change; latent heat → phase change at constant T.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe the three modes of heat transfer.
questions.reference_answer: (1) Conduction: heat flows through material by molecular collisions, no bulk motion. (2) Convection: heat transfer by bulk movement of heated fluid. (3) Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (infrared), no medium needed.
questions.grading_criteria: All three modes named and correctly described.

questions.question: 100 g of water at 90°C is mixed with 150 g of water at 30°C. Find the final temperature.
questions.grading_criteria: T_f = 54°C with correct heat balance equation.

questions.question: State the first law of thermodynamics. What is internal energy?
questions.reference_answer: First law: ΔU = Q - W. Internal energy U is the total molecular energy stored in the system (kinetic + potential of all molecules). It is a state function — depends only on thermodynamic state, not on how it was reached.
questions.grading_criteria: ΔU = Q - W; internal energy explained as state function.

questions.question: Compare isothermal and adiabatic processes for an ideal gas.
questions.reference_answer: Isothermal: ΔT=0, ΔU=0, Q=W, PV=const (slow process). Adiabatic: Q=0, ΔU=-W, PVγ=const (fast process, temperature changes).
questions.grading_criteria: Correct comparison of Q, ΔU, W for each; PV const vs PVγ const.

questions.question: State the second law of thermodynamics — both Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements.
questions.reference_answer: Kelvin-Planck: No engine can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. Clausius: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot body without external work. Both statements are equivalent.
questions.grading_criteria: Both statements correctly given; equivalence confirmed.

questions.question: A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J per cycle. Find efficiency, work done, and heat rejected.
State the ideal gas equation. What are the key assumptions of kinetic theory for ideal gases?
questions.reference_answer: PV = nRT (or PV = NkT). Key assumptions: molecules are point masses, in random motion, collisions perfectly elastic, no intermolecular forces between collisions, molecular size negligible vs separation.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct equation; at least 4 assumptions stated.

questions.question: State the law of equipartition of energy and use it to find Cv for a monatomic ideal gas.
questions.reference_answer: Each degree of freedom has average energy ½kT. Monatomic gas has 3 translational DOF → U = 3kT/2 per molecule. Cv = dU/dT per mole = 3R/2 ≈ 12.5 J/mol·K.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct law; Cv = 3R/2 derived for monatomic gas.

questions.question: Find the rms speed of nitrogen molecules at 27°C. (M = 28 g/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol·K)
questions.grading_criteria: v_rms ≈ 517 m/s using v_rms = √(3RT/M).

questions.question: Define Simple Harmonic Motion. Write the displacement equation and expression for time period.
questions.reference_answer: SHM: F = -kx (restoring force proportional to displacement, directed toward equilibrium). x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ). T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k).
questions.grading_criteria: F = -kx; x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ); T = 2π√(m/k).

questions.question: What is the time period of a simple pendulum? On what factors does it depend and what is it independent of?
questions.reference_answer: T = 2π√(L/g). Depends on L and g. Independent of: mass of bob, amplitude (for small angles < ~15°), material.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct formula; mention independence from mass and small-angle condition.

questions.question: A spring of k = 500 N/m has a 200 g mass. Find time period and frequency of oscillation.
What is resonance? Why can it be both useful and dangerous? Give one example of each.
questions.reference_answer: Resonance: driving frequency = natural frequency → very large amplitude. Useful: radio tuning circuits. Dangerous: Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse (1940) from wind-driven resonance; soldiers break step on bridges.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct definition; one useful and one dangerous example.

questions.question: Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves with an example of each.
questions.reference_answer: Transverse: particle oscillation ⊥ wave propagation (e.g., string waves, EM waves). Longitudinal: particle oscillation ∥ propagation (e.g., sound in air). Longitudinal waves produce compressions and rarefactions.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct distinction with direction of oscillation; correct examples.

questions.question: Explain the general equation y(x,t) = A sin(kx - ωt), identifying all terms.
questions.reference_answer: A = amplitude. k = 2π/λ = wave number. ω = 2πf = angular frequency. (kx - ωt) = phase. Wave speed v = ω/k = λf. Describes wave moving in +x direction.
questions.grading_criteria: All terms defined: A, k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf, v = ω/k = λf.

questions.question: What are standing waves? How are nodes and antinodes formed?
questions.reference_answer: Standing waves: superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions. Nodes: points of zero displacement (destructive interference, always cancel). Antinodes: maximum displacement (constructive interference). Adjacent nodes separated by λ/2.
questions.grading_criteria: Formation by superposition; nodes (zero) and antinodes (max) correctly identified; λ/2 spacing.

questions.question: State the Doppler effect and write the formula for observed frequency when both source and observer are moving.
questions.reference_answer: Doppler effect: apparent change in frequency due to relative source-observer motion. f_obs = f_source × (v ± v_obs)/(v ∓ v_src). Approaching → higher f (blueshift); receding → lower f (redshift).
questions.grading_criteria: Correct formula with sign conventions; blueshift/redshift noted.

questions.question: A 1 m string fixed at both ends vibrates in its 3rd harmonic at wave speed 200 m/s. Find the frequency.
questions.grading_criteria: f₃ = 300 Hz using λ₃ = 2L/3.

questions.question: A 3 kg block slides down a frictionless 30° incline of length 4 m. Find: (a) work by gravity, (b) speed at bottom, (c) power delivered by gravity if it takes 2 s. (g = 10 m/s²)
Atwood's machine: masses 4 kg and 6 kg over a frictionless pulley. Find (a) acceleration and (b) string tension. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.reference_answer: (a) a = (m₂-m₁)g/(m₁+m₂) = 2×10/10 = 2 m/s². (b) T = m₁(g+a) = 4×12 = 48 N (verified: T = m₂(g-a) = 6×8 = 48 N).
questions.grading_criteria: a = 2 m/s², T = 48 N with verification.

questions.question: What is a geostationary satellite? Derive the expression for its orbital radius.
questions.reference_answer: Geostationary satellite: orbits in equatorial plane with T = 24 h, appears stationary. Derivation: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r → r³ = GMT²/4π² → r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m ≈ 42,000 km.
questions.grading_criteria: Definition; derivation of r³ = GMT²/4π²; value ≈ 42,000 km.

questions.question: Why is the efficiency of a real heat engine always less than a Carnot engine operating between the same temperatures?
questions.reference_answer: Carnot engine uses reversible processes → maximum efficiency η = 1 - T_C/T_H. Real engines have irreversibilities (friction, turbulence, non-quasi-static processes), each generating entropy. By the second law, no engine can exceed Carnot efficiency; irreversibilities always reduce actual efficiency below the ideal.
questions.grading_criteria: Carnot = reversible; real = irreversible; entropy generation; second law upper bound.

questions.chapter_title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: State and explain the parallel axis theorem.
questions.reference_answer: I = I_cm + Md², where I = moment of inertia about any axis, I_cm = moment about parallel axis through centre of mass, M = total mass, d = perpendicular distance between axes.
questions.grading_criteria: Correct theorem I = I_cm + Md²; d identified as distance between parallel axes.

questions.question: Using kinetic theory, explain why pressure of an ideal gas increases with temperature at constant volume.
questions.reference_answer: P = (1/3)ρv²_rms. Since ½mv²_rms = 3kT/2, v²_rms ∝ T. At constant V, higher T → higher molecular speeds → more frequent, harder wall collisions → higher pressure. Thus P ∝ T (Gay-Lussac's law) from kinetic theory.
questions.grading_criteria: v²_rms ∝ T; increased collision frequency and force; P ∝ T conclusion.
